newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's coffee growers step up import protest.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's coffee growers step up import protest.

text.p: Mexican coffee farmers are clamoring for the government to halt inward shipments of low quality robusta beans, crying foul on a new tariff-free import quota they say will badly hurt the home-grown business.
"It's as if someone's come into your house and told you you've been kicked out of your room," Mexican Coffee Grower Confederation member Alejandro Garcia Palacios told Reuters.
At Monday's National Farm Council (CNA) annual assembly, Garcia asked Agriculture Minister Francisco Labastida to halt coffee imports and reconsider the tariff-free quota.
"We are asking you to stop the decision to import so that it does not affect coffee farmers in the countryside," Garcia said.
Mexico is considered the world's fourth largest coffee producer, with 5.1 million 60-kg bags in the 1996-1997 crop.

Coffee growers in Mexico have traditionally griped over the some 90,000 60-kg bags the country imports per year. But now growers say the salt on this wound is a new 150,000 60-kg bag import quota for 1997, free of tariffs, which they say they weren't consulted over.
Labastida told Garcia no coffee has yet been imported under the new tariff-free scheme, but producers remain dubious.

For four months growers have been hammering at the government to cancel the tariff-free import quota, confederation executive director Juan Carlos Villareal said. So far the pleas have fallen on deaf ears.
"They say the coffee is imported and re-exported with added value. That's not true," he said.

Growers claim roasters are trying to avoid paying current high coffee prices by importing poorer quality beans for mass soluble consumption. Roasters asked Mexico's Trade Ministry to create the tariff-free coffee import quota, producers said.
"The imports are unnecessary. We supply enough coffee to satisfy the domestic market and for exports," Garcia said. "Why is there a demand for imported coffee? That's the question."
Ruben Castillo, executive president of the government's Mexican Coffee Council, told Reuters earlier this month that the exports were minimal and not a concern to the council.
He said the council does not oppose the exports, but would prefer to replace them with coffee from Mexico. "We should stop worrying about (the imports), and instead take action to replace them."
